title: Notebook 04 — Results and Figures
text:
Question: what does the detector produce for each of the three runs, and which single figure shows it?
Generates the per-test summary dashboards and one comparison figure across all three runs, then writes a raw detection summary.
The lead-time and downtime-cost analysis is deliberately not here. It needs a sustained-alert rule and a false-alarm rate calibrated on a healthy baseline, which business.py adds. The intervals this notebook prints are raw first-alert numbers and are labelled as such.
Code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

from nasa_bearing_anomaly.business import (
    PUBLISHED_HOURLY_COST,
    DowntimeCostModel,
    compute_lead_time,
    cost_sensitivity,
    format_result,
)
from nasa_bearing_anomaly.config import (
    FIGURES_DIR,
    HEADLINE_DIR,
    REPORTS_DIR,
    TEST_CONFIG,
    repo_path,
)
from nasa_bearing_anomaly.detection import run_pipeline, select_features
from nasa_bearing_anomaly.plotting import BearingPlotter

# Output directories come from config, which resolves them against the package
# location rather than the working directory. The relative literals these replaced
# ("../results/figures") were correct only when the kernel happened to start in
# notebooks/, and silently wrote elsewhere when it did not.
for d in (FIGURES_DIR, REPORTS_DIR, HEADLINE_DIR):

text:
1. Score All Three Runs
Detection is re-run here rather than read back from results/reports/*_results.csv. Those scored frames are gitignored, so on a fresh clone they are absent — and a cell that reads them when present and recomputes when not would produce different numbers depending on what happened to be on disk.
The feature table is pinned to the enriched one for the same reason. It is written by notebook 02, so run these in order; pinning it means a missing table raises instead of silently falling back to the narrower committed table, which selects 4 feature columns instead of 20 and fits a different model.


Code
FEATURE_SOURCE = "enriched"

for test_id in [1, 2, 3]:
    results[test_id] = run_pipeline(test_id, feature_source=FEATURE_SOURCE)

# first flagged file, which is file 0 in all three runs -- so the README's hero image

lead_results = [
    compute_lead_time(df, test_id, feature_source=FEATURE_SOURCE) for test_id, df in results.items()

lead_by_test = {r.test_id: r for r in lead_results}

text:
3. All-Tests Comparison Figure
One clean figure showing all 3 tests side by side — for README header.


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(18, 13))
fig.patch.set_facecolor("#0d1117")
fig.suptitle(
    "NASA IMS Bearing Dataset — Predictive Maintenance via Anomaly Detection\n"
    "All Three Test Runs | Isolation Forest | Sustained-alert rule, 1% calibrated FAR",
    fontsize=13,
    fontweight="bold",
    color="#e6edf3",
    y=0.99,
)

bearing_colors = ["#58a6ff", "#3fb950", "#d29922", "#bc8cff"]

for row, (test_id, df) in enumerate(results.items()):
    config = TEST_CONFIG[test_id]
    failed = config["failed_bearing"]
    rms_col = f"{failed}_ch1_rms"
    lead = lead_by_test[test_id]

    ax_rms = axes[row, 0]
    ax_score = axes[row, 1]

    for ax in [ax_rms, ax_score]:
        ax.set_facecolor("#161b22")

    # ── Left: All bearings RMS ──
    for i, bearing in enumerate(["Bearing1", "Bearing2", "Bearing3", "Bearing4"]):
        col = f"{bearing}_ch1_rms"
        if col in df.columns:
            lw = 1.5 if bearing == failed else 0.6
            alpha = 1.0 if bearing == failed else 0.5
            lbl = bearing + (" (failed)" if bearing == failed else "")
            ax_rms.plot(
                df.index, df[col], color=bearing_colors[i], linewidth=lw, alpha=alpha, label=lbl
            )

    ax_rms.set_title(
        f"Test {test_id}: RMS — {config['failure_mode']}",
        fontsize=10,
        color="#e6edf3",
        fontweight="bold",
    )
    ax_rms.set_ylabel("RMS (g)", color="#e6edf3")
    ax_rms.legend(fontsize=7, loc="upper left")
    ax_rms.grid(True, color="#30363d", alpha=0.6)
    ax_rms.tick_params(colors="#e6edf3")

    # ── Right: Detection result, marked at the SUSTAINED alarm ──
    if rms_col in df.columns:
        ax_score.plot(df.index, df[rms_col], color="#58a6ff", linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.7, label="RMS")

        if "is_anomaly" in df.columns:
            anom_mask = df["is_anomaly"]
            ax_score.scatter(
                df.index[anom_mask],
                df[rms_col][anom_mask],
                color="#f85149",
                s=6,
                zorder=5,
                alpha=0.5,
                label="Flagged file (raw)",
            )

        # The post-shutdown tail is measured per run, not assumed to be one file.
        if lead.n_shutdown_dropped:
            ax_score.axvspan(
                df.index[len(df) - lead.n_shutdown_dropped],
                df.index[-1],
                color="#6e7681",
                alpha=0.35,
                label=f"Post-shutdown ({lead.n_shutdown_dropped})",
            )

        if lead.alarm_file is not None:
            ax_score.axvline(
                x=lead.alarm_file,
                color="#3fb950",
                linestyle="--",
                linewidth=1.8,
                label=f"Sustained alarm ({lead.k}-of-{lead.m})",
            )
            ax_score.text(
                lead.alarm_file - max(2, len(df) * 0.01),
                ax_score.get_ylim()[1] * 0.70 if ax_score.get_ylim()[1] > 0 else 0.5,
                f"{lead.lead_hours:.0f} h warning\nfile {lead.alarm_file} of {len(df)}",
                color="#3fb950",
                fontsize=8,
                fontweight="bold",
                ha="right",
            )

        ax_score.axvline(
            x=lead.anchor_file, color="#f85149", linestyle="-", linewidth=1.5, label="Failure"
        )

    ax_score.set_title(
        f"Test {test_id}: {lead.lead_hours:.0f} h warning, 0 false alarms in "
        f"{lead.heldout_files} healthy files",
        fontsize=10,
        color="#e6edf3",
        fontweight="bold",
    )
    ax_score.set_ylabel(f"{failed} RMS (g)", color="#e6edf3")
    ax_score.legend(fontsize=7, loc="upper left")
    ax_score.grid(True, color="#30363d", alpha=0.6)
    ax_score.tick_params(colors="#e6edf3")

for ax in axes[-1]:
    ax.set_xlabel("File Index (Time →)", color="#e6edf3")

plt.tight_layout()
out_path = FIGURES_DIR / "all_tests_comparison.png"
plt.savefig(out_path, dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight", facecolor="#0d1117")
print(f"Saved: {repo_path(out_path)}")
plt.show()

section: 4. Lead Time and Its False-Alarm Cost
text:
4. Lead Time and Its False-Alarm Cost
business.py owns this metric; the cell below only renders it. That split is deliberate — an earlier version of this notebook computed lead time inline, and an inline copy of a metric drifts from the module until the two report different numbers with equal confidence.
What the module does, and why each step is needed, is in its docstring. In short: the is_anomaly column cannot be used as an alarm, because contamination fixes the fraction of healthy training files labelled anomalous, so a metric triggering on the first flag just measures the length of the run. The threshold is instead calibrated on healthy data to a chosen false-alarm rate, a k-of-m sustained rule is chosen against healthy data alone, and the post-shutdown tail is measured rather than assumed to be one file.

What the warning is worth
Lead time is not multiplied by an hourly rate. That prices hours during which the machine was still running normally, and it is the mistake the earlier inline version made.
Warning converts an unplanned stoppage into a planned one, so the saving is the difference between the two stoppage lengths — and it is realised only if the warning is long enough to order the part and book a window. Past that point a longer warning does not save more money, which is why the figures below are flat across all three tests.
Every number in the model is an assumption, not a measurement, so the rate is varied rather than asserted. The published whole-facility figures printed underneath are there for scale only: a single bearing is not a whole plant, and the gap between the two is the point.

title: Notebook 02 — Feature Engineering
text:
Question: which quantities actually separate a healthy bearing from a failing one, and why should they?
The model is not what makes this work — an Isolation Forest over raw RMS is a few lines. What decides whether it detects anything early is which quantities it is given. This notebook builds two sets, and only the second currently reaches the detector:
The first set needs a raw waveform and the pipeline reads the summary table, so nothing in it reaches the model. Joining the two is the next piece of work; until then this notebook shows what those features do, not what they contribute.
Not all of them move in the direction intuition suggests. Where they do not, the direction is stated next to the feature and pinned by a test.

1.1 Time-Domain Features


Code
# Simulate healthy vs faulty bearing signals to demonstrate features
np.random.seed(42)
fs = 20000
t = np.linspace(0, 1, fs)

# Healthy: Gaussian noise + harmonic
healthy = np.random.normal(0, 0.1, fs) + 0.05 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 33.33 * t)

# Faulty: Add periodic impulses at BPFO = 236 Hz
bpfo = 236.0
impulse_times = np.arange(0, 1, 1 / bpfo)
faulty = healthy.copy()
for it in impulse_times:
    idx = int(it * fs)
    if idx < fs - 100:
        faulty[idx : idx + 50] += np.random.exponential(0.8) * np.exp(-np.linspace(0, 5, 50))

extractor = FeatureExtractor(fs=fs)

# Frequency domain (FFT)
def plot_fft(ax, x, fs, color, title):
    N = len(x)
    freqs = fftfreq(N, 1 / fs)[: N // 2]
    mag = np.abs(fft(x))[: N // 2] * 2 / N
    ax.semilogy(freqs, mag + 1e-6, color=color, linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.8)
    ax.set_xlim(0, 2000)
    ax.set_title(title, fontweight="bold")
    ax.set_xlabel("Frequency (Hz)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Magnitude")
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

1.2 Frequency-Domain Features
Spectral Entropy measures how evenly energy is spread across frequency: - Healthy: broadband, near-Gaussian noise — energy spread evenly → high entropy - Faulty: energy concentrates at BPFO/BPFI harmonics — sharp peaks → lower entropy
This runs opposite to the intuition that damage means more chaos. The impulses a defect produces are periodic, so they add structure to the spectrum rather than removing it. The direction is verified against the synthetic signals below and asserted in tests/test_features.py.
Because entropy falls for a reason that other things can also cause, read it alongside defect-frequency band energy rather than on its own.

text:
3. Rolling Features — The Trend Signal
A rolling mean smooths noise and reveals the degradation trend. Rate-of-change detects acceleration in degradation — often the earliest warning.


Code

title: What the warning is worth
text: The tempting move is to take 79.5 hours of warning, multiply by a cost-per-hour of downtime, and report the product as money saved. That number would be wrong, and wrong in a way that inflates it.

title: What the warning is worth
section: The intuitive calculation answers the wrong question
text:
The intuitive calculation answers the wrong question
79.5 hours × €15,000/h = €1.19 m looks like a result. It prices 79.5 hours during which the machine was still running normally. Nothing was lost in those hours and nothing was saved by them.
Warning does not save the warning period. It converts an unplanned stoppage into a planned one: the part is ordered before it is needed, the repair happens in a scheduled window, and nobody diagnoses a failure under pressure with the line down. So the saving is the difference between two stoppage lengths — and it is realised only if the warning arrives early enough to act on. A two-hour warning buys nothing when the spare takes a day to arrive.

title: Method
text:
The model here is ordinary — a scikit-learn Isolation Forest, which is the most common choice made on this dataset. What the project rests on is not the model but the layer after it: a lead-time metric built so that it cannot be tuned into a flattering number.
The feature scope, stated up front. The features below fall into two groups: those the published pipeline actually scores, and the defect-frequency machinery that is implemented and tested but not yet joined to it. The second group needs raw waveforms, and the pipeline scores a table of per-file summary statistics, so nothing in it reaches the model. The split is marked throughout, because the difference between what this project measures and what it is set up to measure is exactly the kind of thing a method page exists to be honest about.

title: Method
section: Why a bearing defect has a frequency
text:
Why a bearing defect has a frequency
A rolling-element bearing is a machine with known geometry, so a defect in it does not produce generic “vibration”. Each rolling element strikes the defect once per pass, and the pass rate follows from the geometry and shaft speed alone. Four rates matter, one per defect location:








Frequency
Struck by
Indicates




BPFO — ball pass frequency, outer race
each ball passing a fixed outer-race point
outer-race spall


BPFI — ball pass frequency, inner race
each ball passing a point on the rotating inner race
inner-race spall


BSF — ball spin frequency
a defect on a ball itself, once per rotation
rolling-element defect


FTF — fundamental train frequency
the cage rotating
cage damage



The data documentation carries the numbers: rig geometry, the four frequencies it yields for this bearing, their provenance, and which one carries the signal in which test. They are properties of the rig rather than choices made here, so they live with the data and are stated once.
This is what would make a fault locatable rather than merely detectable. Energy rising at the outer-race pass frequency and its harmonics says outer race — it does not say “something is wrong”. That is what the frequency-domain features are built to see, and it is the part not yet wired into the published result.

title: Method
text:
What the detector reads
loading.py reduces each 20,480-sample acquisition to six statistics per channel: RMS, mean, standard deviation, absolute maximum, excess kurtosis and skewness. features.py then adds, for the RMS and kurtosis columns only, rolling mean, standard deviation and maximum over windows of 10 and 50 files, plus first differences and their absolute values.
The detector selects from that table by substring — _rms, _kurt, _std, _max — and by the failed bearing’s prefix. Mean and skewness are computed and then not selected. For Test 3, Bearing 3 that is 20 columns; for Test 1, which carries two accelerometers per bearing, 40.

RMS — total vibration energy. The primary degradation indicator, and on this data it rises 11.4× above baseline before Test 3’s bearing fails.
Kurtosis — the fourth moment, sensitive to impulsiveness rather than amplitude. A spall produces sharp repeated impacts, which raise kurtosis while RMS is still near baseline, so it can lead RMS. Note this project computes excess kurtosis, where Gaussian reads 0 and not 3 — every threshold in the bearing literature is quoted 3 too high for this column. See the data documentation.
Standard deviation and absolute maximum — for a near-zero-mean signal the first is numerically close to RMS, and the second is the peak that a crest factor would be built from.
The rolling and difference columns are 16 of the 20. They carry the rate of degradation rather than its level, which is what lets an alert fire while the level itself is still unremarkable.

Every one of these is a time-domain quantity. None of them knows what a bearing is.

title: Method
section: Implemented, and not yet joined to the pipeline
text:
Implemented, and not yet joined to the pipeline
FeatureExtractor computes the following from a raw 1-D waveform. Each is exercised by tests/test_features.py, and notebook 02 demonstrates them on synthetic healthy and faulty signals — but the detection pipeline never loads a waveform, so none of them appears in the feature table the model sees.
Frequency domain, from a Welch power spectral density (PSD) estimate:

Defect-frequency band energy — power in narrow bands around BPFO, BPFI, BSF and FTF and their first three harmonics. This is the physics-informed feature proper: it asks the specific question the geometry poses.
Spectral entropy — how evenly energy is spread across the spectrum.
High-frequency ratio — proportion of energy above 5 kHz.

Time domain, shape ratios the summary table does not carry:

Crest factor and clearance factor — peak-to-average ratios, the same impulsiveness idea as kurtosis, normalised differently.

Joining these to the pipeline costs one pass over the 6.2 GB raw archive. Whether they earn their place over RMS and kurtosis alone is then an ablation rather than an assertion, and that experiment has not been run.

title: Method
section: Three feature directions that are the opposite of the intuition
text:
Three feature directions that are the opposite of the intuition
These are properties of the features in the section above — established on synthetic signals and by the test suite, not measured on this dataset’s published result, since none of them is in it. Each is a trap that produces a confidently wrong reading, so they are worth stating plainly, together with how firmly each is actually established, which differs between them.

Spectral entropy is higher in healthy bearings, not lower. The intuition says a fault means disorder means high entropy. The opposite holds: healthy bearing noise is broadband and close to flat, which is maximum entropy. A developing defect concentrates energy into BPFO harmonics — structure, not noise — and structure lowers entropy. This one is pinned by a test (test_spectral_entropy_faulty_lower_than_healthy, asserting healthy > faulty on synthetic signals), so it cannot silently regress.
high_freq_ratio runs the other way too, for the same underlying reason: healthy Gaussian noise is already rich in high frequencies, so there is little headroom for a fault to add any. Only the [0, 1] range is asserted by a test; the direction is documented but not pinned.
crest_factor becomes unreliable at high fault severity. The standard explanation is that it rises early, as discrete impacts appear against a quiet floor, then falls back once the defect is severe enough that impacts merge into a noise floor the fault itself has lifted — so the peak stops standing out from the average. Read monotonically, it will eventually suggest the bearing is recovering. Only crest_factor >= 1 is asserted by a test; the non-monotonicity is a documented caution here, not a measurement this project makes.

The uneven footing is deliberate to record rather than paper over: one direction is enforced by the suite, two are conventions carried from the literature and the feature definitions. Anything relying on the latter two should re-derive them first.

title: Method
text:
The detector
StandardScaler → PCA (10 components) → IsolationForest, fitted on the first 60% of each series on the assumption that a run-to-failure rig starts healthy, then scoring the whole series. Isolation Forest suits the problem because it needs no labels and isolates outliers by random partitioning, which is cheap and explainable.
An autoencoder path exists (PyTorch, optional install) and is handled correctly by the metric layer, including its inverted sign convention. No autoencoder result is published: it did not earn a place over the Isolation Forest on this data.

title: Method
section: Turning scores into an alert, without cheating
text:
Turning scores into an alert, without cheating
This is the part that took the work. Three problems have to be solved in order, and each one is a precondition for the next.

1. is_anomaly cannot be used at all
contamination=c guarantees that fraction of the training window is labelled anomalous, and the training window is the part assumed healthy. Measured: 5.03%, 5.08% and 8.01% of training files flagged, against configured 0.05, 0.05 and 0.08. So the label is doing what it was asked to do, and the first flagged file lands at or near file 0 on every run. The lead time is therefore read from a score threshold, never from is_anomaly.


2. A single flagged window is not an alert
Runs of consecutive flags occur by chance at those rates — a 10-of-10 rule still fires at file 9 of Tests 2 and 3. The rule is k of the last m files flagged.


3. Choosing k and m is where a result gets fabricated
Picking the (k, m) that yields the nicest lead time is precisely the failure the sustained rule exists to prevent, and it would be invisible in the output. Two things prevent it here:
The candidate list is fixed in advance, ordered by window length then strictness — 3-of-5, 4-of-5, 5-of-5, 6-of-10, … 30-of-30 — and the first entry that does not fire on healthy data wins. That is the most sensitive rule meeting the constraint, not the best-scoring one. Lead time is never consulted during selection.
The healthy region is split into three disjoint windows, so no window both sets a parameter and scores it:








Window
Slice of the live series
Job




Calibration
first 10%
sets the score threshold, at a 1% per-file false-alarm rate


Selection
10% – 25%
chooses k and m


Held out
25% – 40%
reports the false-alarm rate — never touched before this



The reported “0 false alarms in 323 / 147 / 949 files” comes from the third window only, which is what makes it out-of-sample.
The 40% boundary is itself an assumption — a run that degraded early would push the “healthy” window into the failure and report a real detection as a false positive — so it is checked rather than assumed: check_healthy_region verifies RMS stays below 2× baseline throughout. All three runs pass.


4. The post-shutdown tail
Each rig auto-terminates on a debris-triggered switch, and the acquisitions after that read near-zero RMS on every channel. They are not healthy readings, and they must not anchor a lead time. The tail is measured per run, not assumed — 0 files for Test 1, 2 for Test 2, 1 for Test 3 — by requiring every bearing to fall below 0.2× baseline, because one bearing can go quiet through damage but all four go quiet only when the shaft stops. Test 1 never went quiet at all and ends on its RMS peak, so the usual “drop the last file” would have discarded the very failure being measured. Details in the data documentation.

title: Method
text:
What this does not establish

The detector uses no frequency-domain feature. Everything it scores is a time-domain statistic or a rolling transform of one. The defect-frequency machinery is implemented and tested but not joined to the pipeline, so this result neither supports nor refutes the claim that bearing kinematics improve early detection. Connecting the two, and ablating the difference, is the next piece of work.
Three runs is three samples. The alert rule is selected per run against that run’s own healthy data. That is correct procedure, and it is not the same as validating a fixed rule on an unseen rig.
Zero false alarms is an upper bound. 147 to 949 held-out files cannot resolve a rate below roughly 1 in 1,000.
Lead time is anchored on the end of the run. The rigs ran to destruction, so the last live acquisition is taken as the failure — but no independent ground-truth failure timestamp exists to check that against, and it ties the number to when the rig happened to stop.

title: Predicting bearing failure before it happens
text:
A rolling-element bearing on a production line fails gradually and then suddenly. The question this project asks is narrow and answerable: using only vibration data, and without a single failure label, how much warning can you get — and what does that warning cost in false alarms?
Both halves matter. A detector that fires early is worthless if it also fires on healthy machinery, and most of the difficulty here turns out to be in the second half rather than the first.

The finding that changed the method
The obvious lead-time metric is “when did the detector first flag something?” On this data that metric is not merely noisy — it is structurally meaningless, and it can be shown to be:

Every run alerts on its very first acquisition, so the “lead time” is just the length of the run. This is not a bug. How k and m are chosen without fitting them to a flattering answer is the subject of the method page.

text:
4. Kurtosis Analysis
Why kurtosis?
Kurtosis measures how heavy a distribution’s tails are — how much of the signal’s energy sits in rare, large excursions rather than in the bulk. A healthy bearing is broadband noise, close to Gaussian. When a race spalls, every rolling element passing the defect produces an impact, and those impacts are exactly the rare large excursions kurtosis responds to. It can move before RMS does, because a handful of impulses barely shifts the total energy.
These columns hold excess kurtosis, so Gaussian reads 0, not 3. The computation subtracts 3 (Fisher definition). Bearing-diagnostics papers normally quote the non-excess value, which makes every published threshold 3 too high for this column:



State
As published (non-excess)
This column (excess)




Healthy, near-Gaussian
3
0


Early fault
5
2


Severe fault
10
7



Getting this backwards puts the “healthy” reference line right where the failure begins. Measured values and the convention are documented in data/README.md.

title: Notebook 03 — Anomaly Detection
text:
1. Why Isolation Forest?
Core idea: Normal data points are hard to isolate — they live in dense clusters and require many splits to separate. Anomalous points are easy to isolate — they’re in sparse regions and need fewer splits.
The algorithm builds random trees and measures the average path length to isolate each point. Short path → anomaly.
Advantages for this problem: - No labels required - Scales well to many features - Robust to the different failure signatures in Tests 1/2/3 - Interpretable anomaly score

title: Notebook 03 — Anomaly Detection
text:
Summary
The Isolation Forest separates the failed bearing from its healthy history on every run. What it does not do is hand over a lead time: the numbers printed above trigger on the first flagged file, and that file is index 0 on all three runs.
That is not a tuning problem. IsolationForest(contamination=c) labels that fraction of its training window anomalous by construction, and the training window is the first 60% — the part assumed healthy. Measured: 5.03% / 5.08% / 8.01% of training files flagged against 0.05 / 0.05 / 0.08 configured. So the raw “lead time” is just the run length, and no choice of model changes that — the autoencoder above lands at 0 as well.
Three things convert it into something usable, all of them in business.py:

a sustained-alert rule, k of the last m files flagged, with k and m chosen on a healthy window that is disjoint from the one the rate is reported on
a score threshold calibrated on held-out healthy data, never is_anomaly
the post-shutdown tail excluded, measured per run rather than assumed — 0 files for Test 1, 2 for Test 2, 1 for Test 3

Applied, those give 79.5 / 53.7 / 57.0 hours of warning against 0 sustained alarms in 323 / 147 / 949 held-out healthy files. Notebook 04 computes and reports them.
